title: Bring the Shoes. Bring Your Real Life: A Better Tailoring Appointment for Two
subtitle: A companion can help you prepare, remember the details and feel less alone. The person being fitted still makes every decision.

body: Make the appointment about the person wearing the clothes

A tailoring appointment can feel unusually exposing: you stand still while someone studies how fabric falls, then try to explain what you want changed. Bringing a partner or friend may make the visit feel more manageable, but their role is support—not evaluation. The person being fitted chooses what feels good, what they want to preserve and whether a proposed adjustment is right for them. No one needs a companion, and a solo appointment is just as valid. The idea here is simply to make a shared visit more useful: one person tries on the garment and leads the conversation; the other can carry shoes, help remember questions or take notes with permission. That division keeps attention on the wearer’s own preferences instead of inviting comparison or turning a loved one into the fit authority.
Start with a three-question prep card

Before the appointment, write down three things: Where will I wear this? What do I want to keep? What feels uncomfortable or looks off? Specific, ordinary language is enough. “The waistband gaps when I sit,” “I want the jacket to close comfortably,” or “I like the length but not how it catches on my shoes” gives the tailor something concrete to discuss. Guidance for preparing clothes for alterations likewise recommends checking how a garment feels in motion and describing the problem plainly, rather than arriving with technical vocabulary [2]. Add any deadline, previous repair or known damage to the card. If you have a reference photo or a similar garment whose fit you like, bring it if it helps explain your preference. It is a visual aid, not a template you must match.
Pack for the outfit you actually plan to wear

A garment’s fit can change with the shoes and layers that go with it. For trousers, bring the shoes you expect to wear; for a jacket or dress, bring relevant undergarments, a belt or other layers that affect how it sits. A tailor’s fitting guidance specifically recommends bringing the shoes and items connected to the intended outfit [1]. This is not about assembling a perfect look. It is about giving the tailor the conditions in which the garment needs to work. Put the garment, accessories and prep card together the night before, and check whether it needs cleaning or whether you should flag a stain, tear or earlier alteration. Your companion can help carry the pieces or check the list. If something is missing, say so rather than pretending the appointment represents the final outfit.
Explain the occasion, not just the silhouette

“I want this to fit better” is a reasonable start, but context makes the request more useful. Is the garment for a workday spent at a desk, a wedding with hours of standing, a commute, a performance or an evening when you expect to dance? Will you need to sit, walk, raise your arms or move quickly? Tailor Brian Burnett’s fitting guidance emphasizes explaining how a garment will be worn and the wearer’s typical posture [1]. You do not need to predict every moment; name the movements that matter most. Your companion might remind you of a use you have mentioned before, but let the wearer decide which details belong in the conversation. If a reference photo captures the desired mood or length, show it and explain what you like about it. A picture can clarify; it should not override comfort.
During the fitting, stay in your own body

Stand naturally rather than holding yourself in a pose you cannot sustain. Try the movements the garment needs to accommodate: sit, walk, reach or raise your arms. If a pin pulls, a proposed change feels restrictive, or you simply cannot tell whether something is comfortable, say so while you are still being fitted. A first alterations appointment may include pinning and movement checks, and more involved work can require another fitting [3]. Your companion can listen for details you want to remember, but should not answer questions about your comfort for you. A useful prompt from them is, “Would you like me to write that down?” A less useful one is, “That looks better,” before you have decided how it feels. There is no requirement to perform confidence; asking for a pause or clarification is part of giving informed direction.
Agree on the change before you leave

At the end, repeat the requested work back in plain language: what is being adjusted, what is meant to stay as it is, the estimated price and when the garment should be ready. Ask whether a second fitting is expected, especially for more involved alterations; the process may take more than one visit [3]. If a deadline matters, make sure the tailor knows before work begins, not as an afterthought. Iron Press Cleaners’ fitting guidance says to speak up if something feels wrong during pinning and to tell the tailor about a firm deadline up front [3]. As a practical step, ask for the agreed work, price and timing to be clear before work begins. Your companion can note the agreed details or help you check that you have the garment and accessories. The wearer should approve the plan, including any uncertainty about how much fabric or shape will change.
Give the companion a small, clear job

A companion is most helpful when their role is agreed in advance. They might carry the shoes, hold a coat, keep the prep card, take a photo of a pinned detail if the tailor and wearer are comfortable with it, or jot down the timeline. They might also offer feedback—but only when asked, and about the question the wearer actually wants answered. “Can you tell whether the hem looks even from behind?” is an invitation; unsolicited judgments about someone’s body or what they “should” wear are not. Before the appointment, ask: Would you like me to take notes, offer an opinion if you ask, or mostly stay quiet? This small conversation makes support legible without making the visit solemn. If opinions differ, the person wearing the garment gets the final word. That is not a courtesy; it is the point.
Leave with a plan you can use

A good appointment does not have to produce a dramatic transformation. It should leave the wearer clearer about what will happen next and whether the proposed work fits their needs. On the way out, check the written notes, confirm the pickup or follow-up date and make sure the shoes or other pieces you brought come home with you. Later, when the altered garment is ready, test it in the same conditions that shaped the request: wear the intended shoes, sit if sitting mattered, and move as you expect to move. If something still feels wrong, describe the specific point rather than deciding you have failed to explain yourself. A tailor appointment is a conversation with practical limits, not a verdict on your body or your taste. Bringing someone can help hold the details; the clothes, comfort and choices remain yours.
